answer.rationale: p99 write-latency at 5× target with a release 2h ago is the strongest causal signal we have. memory_b1 (day 18) documents that a rollback of a bad release cleared a checkout error spike without customer impact, and memory_b3 (day 47) shows we already provisioned headroom so the settlement-peak write volume can be absorbed while we roll back. Rolling back is the single fastest, lowest-risk lever that restores the write path while the prior build is known-stable; regional failover and circuit-breaker patterns are useful later but add complexity during peak settlement traffic. Rollback preserves all in-flight writes because the prior build handled the same traffic pattern successfully, and the settlement peak itself is not the problem (queue depth stayed flat during a retail peak before), so we don't need to shed load or reroute. Capacity is sufficient for one intervention; rollback is the one that maximizes sustained availability without losing customer writes.
